simple: how long one job takes from start to finish.
analogy: the minutes from reading an order to the bowl on the pass.
precise: the time between the start of an operation (an instruction, a memory access, a request) and the moment its result is available.
source: D2 of F1-55 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many jobs are finished per second when the machine is kept busy.
analogy: bowls leaving the hall per minute.
precise: the rate at which operations complete, measured over many operations; for one functional unit it is bounded by how often it can accept a new operation.
source: D2 of F1-55 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: to finish many jobs per second when each takes a long time, many jobs must be under way at once.
analogy: if each bowl spends ten minutes in the hall and twenty bowls must leave per minute, two hundred bowls are in the hall at any moment.
precise: in a stable system, the average number of items in the system equals their average rate times their average time in the system: L = λW; for latency hiding, the independent operations in flight needed to sustain a throughput against a latency.
source: D4 of F1-55 (Little, "A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: independent steps inside one program that the processor may work on at the same time.
analogy: chopping onions while the stock warms.
precise: the degree to which instructions of a single instruction stream do not depend on each other's results and can overlap; on a GPU, for example several independent loads issued before the first use.
source: D2 of F1-55 (Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: many separate jobs, each with its own steps, that can run side by side.
analogy: hundreds of separate bowls being prepared.
precise: parallelism from multiple independent instruction streams (threads); a GPU exposes it as very many lightweight threads created by one launch and hides latency by switching between their warps.
source: D1 of F1-55 (Hwu, Kirk, El Hajj, "Programming Massively Parallel Processors"); D2 of F1-55 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a processor built to finish one sequence of steps as soon as possible.
analogy: one cook with a well-organised station.
precise: a design that spends chip area and power on reducing the time of a single thread: large caches, branch prediction, out-of-order and speculative execution.
source: D1 and D2 of F1-55 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a processor built to finish as many jobs per second as possible, even if each one is slower.
analogy: the banquet hall full of helpers.
precise: a design that spends area on many simple arithmetic lanes and on keeping many threads resident, and tolerates long latencies by switching to other ready work.
source: D1 of F1-55 (Hwu, Kirk, El Hajj, "Programming Massively Parallel Processors"); D3 of F1-55 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the function every GPU thread runs.
analogy: the recipe card handed to every helper.
precise: a function launched from the host and executed on the device by many threads; in CUDA and HIP it is marked __global__. Not the operating-system kernel.
source: D3 of F1-55 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); compiler evidence R3 of F1-55

simple: a pretend GPU that this course invented so that the arithmetic is easy.
analogy: a model kitchen used in cookery class, not a real restaurant.
precise: an invented GPU with round numbers (4 SMs, warps of 32; per SM 16 resident warps, 4 blocks, 16,384 registers, 32 KiB shared memory; model latencies 100 and 4 cycles; 256-bit memory at 8 GT/s; host link 16 GB/s with 10 µs per copy) used only for worked examples and models; none of its numbers describe a real product.
source: defined in F1-55 of this university (invented; not a source about any GPU)

simple: one of the identical building blocks of an NVIDIA GPU that runs threads.
analogy: one section of the banquet hall with its own table, racks and supervisor.
precise: streaming multiprocessor: NVIDIA's replicated processor unit; thread blocks are scheduled onto SMs, and each SM holds the registers, shared memory and schedulers for its resident warps. The CUDA runtime reports the count as multiProcessorCount.
source: D3 of F1-56 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); H1 of F1-56 (CUDA 12.0 header driver_types.h, read in this build)

simple: AMD's name for the building block that runs threads.
analogy: a section of the hall in AMD's building.
precise: AMD's replicated processor unit, which runs the wavefronts of the workgroups assigned to it, with vector and scalar execution resources, a register file and the LDS; HIP's header describes multiProcessorCount as "Number of multi-processors (compute units)".
source: D6 of F1-56 (AMD "AMD Instinct MI200" ISA reference guide) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); H2 of F1-56 (HIP 5.7 header, read in this build)

simple: a team of GPU threads that always runs together on one SM or CU.
analogy: one group of orders handled at one section.
precise: the group of threads of a launch scheduled as a unit onto one SM (CUDA thread block) or CU (AMD workgroup); its threads can share on-chip memory and synchronise at barriers, and it stays there until all its threads finish.
source: D3 and D8 of F1-56 (CUDA C++ Programming Guide; HIP documentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: already sitting on an SM with everything it needs, ready to run.
analogy: an order whose helpers stand at the section's table.
precise: a block or warp whose registers and on-chip memory are allocated on an SM or CU, so its instructions can be issued with no switching cost; per-SM limits are reported as maxBlocksPerMultiProcessor and maxThreadsPerMultiProcessor.
source: D3 of F1-56 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); H1 of F1-56

simple: one round in which every free place on every SM gets a block.
analogy: one round of seating, when every section's table is filled once.
precise: the set of blocks that can be resident at once across the GPU (SMs × resident blocks per SM); a launch with more blocks runs in several waves, and a partly filled last wave is the tail. Not an AMD wavefront.
source: D1 of F1-56 (Hwu, Kirk, El Hajj, "Programming Massively Parallel Processors") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the name of a GPU's generation that compilers use.
analogy: the edition number printed on the building plan.
precise: NVIDIA identifies a GPU's feature set by a compute capability (major.minor; compiler targets sm_XY and compute_XY); AMD identifies the instruction set by a gfx target name such as gfx90a, reported in gcnArchName.
source: H1 and H2 of F1-56 (CUDA 12.0 and HIP 5.7 headers, read in this build); R4 of F1-56 (nvcc target list)

simple: AMD keeps values that are the same for a whole wavefront in one place and per-thread values in another.
analogy: one note on the board for the whole row, versus each helper's own hands.
precise: on GCN/CDNA targets, scalar registers (SGPRs) hold one value per wavefront for s_ instructions; vector registers (VGPRs) hold one value per lane for v_ instructions; kernel metadata reports .sgpr_count and .vgpr_count.
source: D6 and D7 of F1-56 (MI200 ISA guide; LLVM AMDGPU user guide) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R5 of F1-56 (compiler metadata)

simple: a group of GPU threads that always do the same step at the same time.
analogy: a row of helpers who follow one supervisor's voice.
precise: the group of threads scheduled and executed together with one instruction stream: an NVIDIA warp (32 on the sm_80 target compiled in this build) or an AMD wavefront (64 on gfx90a and gfx942; 32 by default on gfx1030 and gfx1100, 64 with -mwavefrontsize64).
source: D3 of F1-57 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 and R6 of F1-57 (compiler output, this build)

simple: one position in a warp; one thread's slot.
analogy: one helper's place in the row.
precise: the index of a thread within its warp or wavefront (0 to width − 1); lane-indexed bits form the masks used by votes and by the active mask.
source: D3 and D6 of F1-57 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: you write code for one thread; the hardware runs it for a whole row of threads at once.
analogy: one recipe card read aloud to a row.
precise: single instruction, multiple threads: threads are programmed as scalar threads but executed in warps that share instruction issue; divergent threads are handled by masking.
source: D3 of F1-57 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide"); D1 of F1-57 ("Programming Massively Parallel Processors") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a row of on/off switches saying which threads of the warp take part in the current step.
analogy: which helpers in the row have their hands up.
precise: a bit mask with one bit per lane; disabled lanes do not write results. On AMD GCN/CDNA it is the 64-bit EXEC register, changed by instructions such as s_and_saveexec_b64; on NVIDIA it is maintained by hardware and compiler (predicates and convergence).
source: D6 of F1-57 (AMD "AMD Instinct MI200" ISA reference guide) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R5 of F1-57 (gfx90a assembly, this build)

simple: when threads of one warp need different steps, so they take turns.
analogy: the spicy bowls and the creamy bowls in one row.
precise: lanes of a warp or wavefront evaluate a branch differently; the paths run one after the other with complementary masks and the lanes reconverge afterwards; the cost is decided by whether any lane takes each path.
source: D3 and D1 of F1-57 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F1-57 (SIMT model run)

simple: doing a short step for everybody, but each thread only keeps the result meant for it.
analogy: each helper's card says which of the two called steps really counts for them.
precise: guarding individual instructions with a per-lane predicate instead of branching; NVIDIA SASS writes @P0 / @!P0; compilers use it for short divergent paths.
source: D5 of F1-57 (NVIDIA "CUDA Binary Utilities") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F1-57 (SASS, this build)

simple: every thread in the warp says yes or no, and everybody gets the whole list of answers.
analogy: a show of hands written down as a row of ticks.
precise: an intrinsic returning a mask with bit l set if lane l's predicate is true: __ballot_sync(mask, p) returns 32 bits in CUDA; HIP's __ballot(p) returns 64 bits on wave64 targets.
source: D3 and D8 of F1-57 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1, R3 and R5 of F1-57 (compiler output)

simple: how many of the lanes did useful work, on average, per step.
analogy: the share of helpers in the row whose hands moved.
precise: useful lane-slots ÷ (instructions issued × width); 100 % without divergence, lower with it.
source: D1 of F1-57 ("Programming Massively Parallel Processors") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F1-57 (model)

simple: the two levels of NVIDIA GPU code: a portable one and the real machine code.
analogy: the recipe in a general cookbook language, and the version rewritten for one particular kitchen.
precise: PTX is NVIDIA's virtual instruction set, kept in binaries for later compilation; SASS is the machine code of one GPU generation (sm_XY), shown by cuobjdump -sass. Example from this build: PTX mov.u32 %r16, WARP_SZ becomes SASS with the constant 0x20 for sm_80.
source: D4 and D5 of F1-57 (PTX ISA; CUDA Binary Utilities) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F1-57

simple: the fastest storage on the GPU, split so each thread gets its own few boxes.
analogy: each helper's tray.
precise: the per-SM (per-CU) array of 32-bit registers divided among resident threads; a kernel's registers per thread are fixed at compile time; reported as regsPerMultiprocessor ("32-bit registers available per multiprocessor").
source: H1 of F1-58 (CUDA 12.0 header, read in this build); D1 of F1-58 ("Programming Massively Parallel Processors") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small, fast memory that the threads of one block share and manage themselves.
analogy: the team's side table.
precise: on-chip memory allocated per thread block, declared __shared__, visible to all threads of the block for its lifetime; filled and read explicitly, with barriers between; reported as smem by ptxas.
source: D3 of F1-58 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F1-58 (ptxas report)

simple: AMD's name for the fast memory a workgroup shares.
analogy: the side table in AMD's building.
precise: local data share: on-chip memory per workgroup on AMD GPUs, accessed with ds_ instructions; its size per workgroup appears as .group_segment_fixed_size in kernel metadata.
source: D6 and D7 of F1-58 (MI200 ISA guide; LLVM AMDGPU user guide) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F1-58 (gfx90a metadata)

simple: when several threads want different words from the same part of shared memory at once, so they wait in line.
analogy: two helpers reaching into the same drawer for different things.
precise: shared memory is split into banks that each serve one word per cycle; when a warp's accesses hit different words in one bank, the access takes as many passes as the largest number of distinct words in a bank. Padding a tile's rows (pitch 33 instead of 32) removes the column-read conflict in a 32-bank model.
source: D3 of F1-58 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R6 of F1-58 (bank model run)

simple: how full the SM is with warps, compared with how many it could hold.
analogy: how many helpers are in the section, out of the places available.
precise: resident warps per SM ÷ maximum resident warps per SM; limited by registers, shared memory, the warp limit and the block limit, whichever allows fewest blocks.
source: D1 and D3 of F1-58 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R7 of F1-58 (occupancy arithmetic, TG-1 invented limits)

simple: when a thread runs out of registers, the compiler parks values in memory and fetches them back.
analogy: walking to the pantry shelf to park pieces that do not fit on the tray.
precise: per-thread local memory is private in scope but stored in device memory and cached; ptxas reports spill stores and loads in bytes; SASS uses STL/LDL. In this build, a register cap of 16 turned 0 spill bytes into 416 bytes of stores and 572 of loads.
source: D3 of F1-58 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R5 of F1-58 (ptxas reports)

simple: automatic copies of recently used memory near the SM (L1) and shared by the whole GPU (L2).
analogy: the pantry shelves of one section, and the hall's central pantry.
precise: hardware-managed caches between SMs and device memory; the L1 is per SM, the L2 shared by all SMs and placed in front of the memory controllers; the CUDA runtime reports l2CacheSize.
source: H1 of F1-58 (CUDA 12.0 header); D2 of F1-58 ("Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a "wait here until everyone in the block arrives" point.
analogy: the team waits until all ingredients are on the side table.
precise: a block-wide execution and memory barrier; BAR.SYNC in SASS and s_barrier on AMD in this build's compiler output.
source: D3 of F1-58 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 and R4 of F1-58

simple: memory chips stacked on top of each other right next to the GPU, connected by very many wires.
analogy: the warehouse against the back wall with a huge doorway.
precise: High Bandwidth Memory: JEDEC-standardised stacked DRAM with a very wide interface per stack, connected to the processor through the package.
source: J1 of F1-59 (JEDEC HBM standard); D1 of F1-59 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: separate memory chips on the graphics board, each connected by fewer, much faster wires.
analogy: the narrow road with fast carts.
precise: Graphics Double Data Rate SDRAM: a JEDEC family of DRAM devices with narrow, high-data-rate interfaces, placed on the circuit board around the GPU.
source: J2 of F1-59 (JEDEC GDDR6 standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the main memory chips: large, cheap per byte, and slow to start answering.
analogy: the warehouse.
precise: dynamic random-access memory: bits stored as charge in capacitors organised in banks, rows and columns; a read opens a row and streams columns. GPU device memory is DRAM.
source: D2 of F1-59 ("Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many wires carry data at the same time.
analogy: the number of lanes on the road.
precise: the total number of data bits the memory interface transfers in parallel; the CUDA runtime reports memoryBusWidth, "Global memory bus width in bits".
source: H1 of F1-59 (CUDA 12.0 header, read in this build)

simple: how many times per second each wire sends a new bit.
analogy: how many carts per second pass on one lane.
precise: transfers per second per data pin; it can be a multiple of a clock frequency, so a clock in MHz or kHz is not a data rate.
source: D2 of F1-59 ("Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the most bytes per second the memory could ever deliver.
analogy: lanes × carts per lane per second.
precise: (bus width in bits ÷ 8) × data rate; a theoretical upper bound, never a measurement (guide AH-23).
source: D1 of F1-59 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F1-59 (formula run)

simple: two sizes of gigabyte: a thousand million bytes, or 2^30 bytes.
analogy: crates counted in tens or in dozens.
precise: 1 GB = 10^9 bytes; 1 GiB = 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 bytes; 256 GB/s = 238.4 GiB/s. Always state which.
source: guide 13.4 (units rule); R1 of F1-59

simple: extra bits that let the memory detect and fix small errors.
analogy: a checksum on each crate's label.
precise: error-correcting codes stored with the data; on some memories they cost capacity or bandwidth; the CUDA runtime reports ECCEnabled.
source: H1 of F1-59; D2 of F1-59 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of an SM that picks, every cycle, which warp does its next step.
analogy: the supervisor choosing a row.
precise: issue logic that selects, among its resident warps, one whose next instruction has its operands and resources ready, and issues it.
source: D1 and D3 of F1-60 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: doing other useful work while waiting, so the waiting costs no time.
analogy: calling another row while the flour is on its way.
precise: overlapping the latency of operations with the issue of independent instructions from the same warp (ILP) or other warps (TLP), so that issue slots stay busy; needs about λW independent operations in flight (Little's law).
source: D1 and D2 of F1-60 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F1-60 (scheduler model)

simple: a warp that cannot take its next step yet.
analogy: a row whose next step needs flour that has not arrived.
precise: a warp is stalled when its next instruction waits for a result (memory or arithmetic latency), a barrier or a busy unit; profilers classify stall reasons.
source: D3 of F1-60 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: moving from one warp to another takes no extra time.
analogy: each row keeps its own bowls on its own bench.
precise: every resident warp keeps its registers in the register file, so the scheduler can issue from a different warp in the next cycle without saving or restoring state.
source: D1 and D2 of F1-60 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an AMD instruction meaning "wait until at most N of my memory requests are still outstanding".
analogy: "wait until the flour is here before mixing".
precise: a scalar instruction on GCN/CDNA that stalls the wavefront until counters of outstanding operations (vmcnt, lgkmcnt) fall to the given value; in this build the compiler put one s_waitcnt vmcnt(0) after three independent global loads.
source: D6 of F1-60 (AMD "AMD Instinct MI200" ISA reference guide) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F1-60 (gfx90a assembly)

simple: a special part of the GPU that multiplies small blocks of numbers in one go.
analogy: a press that mixes a whole tray in one stroke.
precise: a functional unit in the SM (NVIDIA tensor core) or CU (AMD CDNA matrix core) that executes a matrix multiply-accumulate on small tiles as one warp- or wavefront-wide instruction (HMMA, v_mfma); available only on some targets.
source: D3 and D6 of F1-61 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3, R5 and R6 of F1-61 (compiler output)

simple: multiply two blocks of numbers and add the result to a third.
analogy: one stroke of the press.
precise: D = A × B + C with A of m × k, B of k × n, C and D of m × n; one MMA performs m·n·k multiply-adds.
source: D4 and D6 of F1-61 (PTX ISA; MI200 ISA guide) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the names of the matrix instructions and programming interfaces.
analogy: the press's operating handles.
precise: WMMA (warp matrix multiply-accumulate) is the CUDA C++ API in mma.h and the PTX wmma family; MFMA (matrix fused multiply-add) is the AMD CDNA instruction family v_mfma_*, reachable from HIP through compiler builtins.
source: H1 of F1-61 (CUDA 12.0 crt/mma.h, read in this build); D3, D4 and D6 of F1-61 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 and R5 of F1-61

simple: the piece of a matrix tile that one thread holds in its registers.
analogy: the bowls each helper carries to the press.
precise: in WMMA, an opaque per-thread object holding part of a tile; its layout across lanes is unspecified, so it is loaded and stored with the *_sync functions.
source: D3 of F1-61 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: multiplying with short numbers but adding up with long ones.
analogy: light bowls in, large pots for the running total.
precise: inputs in a short format (FP16, BF16 or shorter), accumulation in a longer format (FP32); in the model of this build, 4,096 ones summed in FP16 give 2,048, in FP32 4,096.
source: D3 of F1-61 — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F1-61 (precision model)

simple: two 16-bit number formats: FP16 keeps more digits, BF16 a wider range.
analogy: two kinds of small bowl: finer markings, or room for more extreme amounts.
precise: IEEE 754 binary16 has an 11-bit significand and 5 exponent bits; bfloat16 has an 8-bit significand and the 8 exponent bits of FP32.
source: D7 of F1-61 (IEEE 754); bfloat16 definition to be sourced — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the standard connection between a computer's processor and plug-in cards such as GPUs.
analogy: the corridor from the main building to the hall.
precise: PCI Express: a point-to-point serial interconnect organised as a tree of links from the root complex through switches to endpoints; on Linux, lspci -tv prints the tree.
source: S1 of F1-62 (PCI-SIG, "PCI Express Base Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F1-62

simple: NVIDIA's faster private connections between GPUs, and the switch chip that joins many GPUs that way.
analogy: private passages between neighbouring kitchens, and a hub where they meet.
precise: NVIDIA's GPU-to-GPU interconnect and the switch that lets every GPU in a node reach every other over it; used for multi-GPU collectives and peer access.
source: S2 of F1-62 (NVIDIA NVLink and NVSwitch documentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: AMD's connections inside and between its chips; xGMI is the version that links GPUs and CPUs to each other.
analogy: AMD's private passages.
precise: AMD's coherent interconnect family; its inter-socket and inter-GPU links are called xGMI.
source: S3 of F1-62 (AMD "AMD CDNA 2 Architecture" whitepaper) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a transfer costs a fixed start-up time plus a time per byte.
analogy: every trolley trip costs the walk, plus the time to roll each crate.
precise: T(n) = α + n/β with α the per-transfer latency and β the bandwidth; small transfers are dominated by α, large ones by n/β; both are measured, not assumed.
source: D2 of F1-62 ("Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F1-62 (copy model)

simple: host memory the operating system promises not to move, so the GPU can read it directly.
analogy: crates already on the loading dock.
precise: host memory locked in physical memory and accessible to the device; the CUDA header says it "can be read or written with much higher bandwidth than pageable memory", and that pageable copies go through "staging memory for DMA transfer".
source: H1 of F1-62 (CUDA 12.0 header cuda_runtime_api.h, read in this build)

simple: a helper on the GPU that moves data over the link by itself while the GPU computes.
analogy: the trolley porters, who work while the cooks cook.
precise: a direct-memory-access engine; asyncEngineCount is 1 when the device can copy between host and device while executing a kernel, 2 when it can copy in both directions and execute a kernel at the same time.
source: H1 of F1-62 (CUDA 12.0 header, read in this build)

simple: one GPU reading or writing another GPU's memory directly.
analogy: passing a crate through the passage to the next kitchen.
precise: direct device-to-device access over PCIe or NVLink/xGMI when the platform allows it; CUDA reports it with cudaDeviceCanAccessPeer.
source: D3 of F1-62 (NVIDIA "CUDA C++ Programming Guide") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the vendor's long document describing how a GPU generation is built.
analogy: the builder's brochure with the floor plan.
precise: a vendor publication describing a GPU architecture or product (block diagrams, unit counts, memory system, features, peak tables); a primary source for architecture whose peak figures carry the vendor's conditions.
source: W1 and W2 of F1-63 (candidate whitepapers) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the biggest number the hardware could reach if everything went perfectly.
analogy: "up to 400 covers an hour".
precise: a figure computed from unit counts, clocks and widths under stated conditions, not measured; an upper bound that is never replaced by a measurement (guide AH-23).
source: guide AH-21 to AH-23 (house rules)

simple: a one-page card listing a GPU's important numbers, each with where it came from.
analogy: a two-column page: what the brochure says, and what was measured.
precise: this course's project: a table of fields for one GPU, each value tagged DOC (document and section), TOOL (tool output run record) or MEAS (measurement run record), or left TBD; checked by F1-63's Listing 1.
source: F1-63 of this university; R1 of F1-63 (checker run)

simple: a short note saying where a number came from.
analogy: the page number next to each copied figure.
precise: the tag in a passport line: DOC: title §section, MEAS: run record, TOOL: run record, or TBD; rules: every value tagged, documents name a section, peaks and measurements kept apart.
source: guide AH-21 to AH-23; R1 and R4 of F1-63 (checker runs)

simple: facts about a GPU that you can read from what the compiler produces, without the GPU.
analogy: learning the size of the trays from the order form for trays.
precise: compiler outputs such as metadata (.wavefront_size: 64), constants substituted for built-ins (MOV R5, 0x20), accepted or rejected instructions and resource reports; they describe the compiler target, not a particular board.
source: R2 of F1-63 (compiler output, this build)

simple: AMD's two GPU families: one for data-centre computing, one for graphics.
analogy: two building plans from the same company, one for banquets and one for restaurants.
precise: CDNA targets (such as gfx90a, gfx942) default to 64-lane wavefronts and have MFMA matrix instructions; RDNA targets (such as gfx1030, gfx1100) default to 32-lane wavefronts and, in this build's compiler, reject the MFMA builtin (needs target feature mai-insts).
source: D6 of F1-57 (AMD "AMD Instinct MI200" ISA reference guide) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R6 of F1-57 and R6 of F1-61 (compiler output, this build)
